Ethan Rewrite:
Recently I made a small recommendation system for movies, and one of the problems I had was figuring out what to recommend when a user had barely rated anything. For people with more ratings it had something to work with, but without that history there wasn't much to tell it what the person would actually like.

The project used a dataset of movie ratings that I cleaned up before trying different ways of making suggestions. I needed to figure out how I wanted to compare the information, so one approach I tried was looking for people who gave similar ratings and using those to suggest movies. Another was based more on how similar the movies were to each other. These didn't always give the same suggestions, which gave me a way to compare what each approach was doing.

While working through this, I got more practice with Python and processing the data, along with the machine learning side of making recommendations. There were things I could get working in the program that still depended on how much information was available for a certain user.

That's where the cold start problem started making more sense to me. I could read about why it happens, but having to deal with a user who didn't have enough ratings made me see what the problem actually meant for my project. The system still needed to suggest something to them, even though it knew much less about them than someone who had rated a lot of movies.

I liked getting to compare the approaches myself and see where they had problems. It gave me more to think about with recommendation systems besides whether the code was running correctly.
